title: Love, the written word and parting remarks
summary: His views on saying I love you, monogamy and a closing drum quip.

people.name: Tom Tom Dick Dick Harry Harry

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Yeah, well it’s got to be felt. How do you define love? I don’t ever tell — a lot of guys, I mean the more you say “I love you” the less it means. I mean ending every phone call to a grandchild or to your son — some people say it ad nauseum. You can’t end your conversation with “I love you.” It’s like Edwin R. Murrow saying “good night and good luck.” And I never say “I love you” to my sons. They don’t need to know that. I don’t need to remind them. I don’t say it to my grandchildren. But I got a Father’s Day card

from my granddaughter and in it she said, “Grandpa I will always love you.” That meant more to me than a thousand phone calls ending with “I love you.” The written word supersedes the spoken word anytime for me. And that’s just the way I see it. But I have a different philosophy in life. I don’t believe in — well I won’t go into that.
That’s just me. But I’ll tell you one thing in parting. What you’ve got about 30 seconds left? A tom-tom can’t be played by every Tom Tom Dick Dick Harry Harry [drums].
